analysis.one_liner: Lets students sue colleges in court instead of being forced into private arbitration.
analysis.headline: The CLASS Act of 2025, a Senate bill to bar colleges from forcing students into arbitration, was referred to the Senate education committee and has not advanced; its 12 sponsors and cosponsors are all Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: Many colleges write clauses into enrollment contracts that require students to settle disputes in private arbitration, waive class-action lawsuits, and give up jury trials. This bill would make those clauses unenforceable and add a condition to federal college funding: no institution may restrict a student's right to bring a claim in court, individually or with others. It would take effect one year after passage.
analysis.who_benefits: Students who are cheated, injured, or otherwise wronged by their college. Today, if a school buries an arbitration clause in its enrollment agreement, a student generally cannot sue in court or join other students in a class action. This bill would restore those options, which matter most in cases where many students are harmed the same way — for example, by misleading job-placement claims or deceptive loan practices — and no single student's losses are large enough to make a solo lawsuit worthwhile.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students with disputes against their colleges

how_it_helps.text: Strips the federal arbitration law from enrollment agreements between students and colleges, so any arbitration clause in those contracts is unenforceable.

Adds a condition to the Higher Education Act requiring institutions to refrain from enforcing any limitation on a student's ability to pursue claims in court, including limits on choice of law, jury trials, and venue, individually or with others.
Takes effect one year after enactment, giving colleges time to remove the clauses from their contracts.

analysis.who_pays: Colleges — particularly those that rely on arbitration clauses to keep disputes out of court — would face lawsuits, class actions, and higher legal costs. Some of that cost could be passed to students through tuition or fees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Colleges, especially those using arbitration clauses

drawbacks.text: Colleges argue that class-action lawsuits are expensive to defend and that the resulting costs could be passed on to all students through tuition, including students who never file a claim.

Critics of ending arbitration note that individual arbitration can be faster and cheaper for a student than years of litigation in court, and that class actions sometimes deliver most of their value to the lawyers; this bill removes that option even when a student might prefer it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change restores a basic legal right: the ability to go to court when a college wrongs you, alone or with other students. The main costs fall on colleges, and some may reach students indirectly through tuition. The strongest objection — that arbitration can be quicker for an individual dispute — is real but does not address the cases class actions are built for, where many students share the same harm and arbitration leaves them with no practical remedy.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which has not taken it up, so it sits waiting with no vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on June 11, 2025, joined by 11 Democratic cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — appears in the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Colleges that use arbitration clauses keep the status quo for now: nothing has changed, so no student gains any new court access under this bill.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its Senate introduction.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor is a Senate Democrat; no Republican has signed on, and the bill has no floor action yet either way.

industries.industry: Colleges and universities, especially for-profit schools
industries.note: The bill would make arbitration and class-action waiver clauses unenforceable in enrollment agreements and condition federal eligibility on dropping them, exposing schools to court litigation. Schools that use these clauses to keep disputes out of court would lose that shield; students gain the court access the shield took away.

College enrollment agreements are a stream of mandated arbitration business; removing these contracts from the federal arbitration law would shrink it. Their interest runs against students seeking open-court remedies.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to committee with no hearing or markup rarely reach the floor, and this one has no Republican cosponsors in a Senate where 60 votes are typically needed to move major legislation. With the HELP Committee showing no action so far this Congress, the bill is likely to remain stalled unless the committee schedules work on it.
